A10.text:
Pact on South China Sea code of conduct unlikely, as ASEAN leaders gather
Finishing negotiations for disputed South China Sea agreement will be a ‘tall order’, analysts say, amid China-Philippines tensions.
A long-awaited pact between the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China for a “code of conduct” in the disputed South China Sea is unlikely to materialise during the regional bloc’s annual gathering of leaders in Manila this week, analysts and officials say.
The agreement would aim to manage tensions and prevent conflict at sea. But talks have dragged on for more than 20 years. In 2023, foreign ministers agreed to work towards finalising the accord within three years.
That deadline fell on 2026 – the year the Philippines took its turn as chair of ASEAN. Under its leadership, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said negotiators have met at least once a month.
But they have fallen short of arriving at a consensus ahead of the summit.
“I just want to say that at this point in time, 80 percent of the document itself is finished,” DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said on Saturday, adding that there are some ‘salient’ points that still need to be ironed out.
She has previously said that geographical scope is one of the contentious issues. Beijing insists it has jurisdiction over nearly the entire South China Sea despite a 2016 international ruling invalidating that claim.
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia also have overlapping territorial claims.
A war of words
The Philippines would also like the accord to respect the rights of countries outside the region, according to DFA spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial. Half of the world’s merchant ships pass through the South China Sea.
But the country may be caught between a rock and a hard place.
“You can’t win it because if you get a good document, you’ll be accused of railroading or it would come across as self-serving. But if it’s a bad document, the Marcos Jr administration will be seen as a weak government,” Aries Arugay, a political scientist at the University of the Philippines, said.
China has consistently accused the United States and its allies, who regularly conduct freedom of navigation operations with the Philippines, of interference.
Tensions between Manila and Beijing have escalated since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. The China Coast Guard has repeatedly deployed water cannon against Philippine vessels and maritime confrontations have resulted in collisions and, on one occasion, a Filipino soldier losing a finger.
In recent weeks, the two countries have been engaged in a war of words.
In September, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s public response to a handwritten note rejecting the 2016 South China Sea ruling – reportedly from Beijing’s military attache in Seoul – went viral.
“Perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do,” Teodoro, who has been barred from entering China, said.
A month later, Beijing’s ambassador to Manila, Jing Quan, told reporters that if China wanted to use force, “we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force. We love peace”. The statement was made in response to a question about Teodoro calling China a “troublemaker”, but which Marcos said “sounded like a threat”.
What followed was a barrage of social media posts by Philippine officials criticising Jing, with the Chinese embassy replying in kind. Senators called for the expulsion of the Chinese envoy.
And, in late October, China accused Teodoro of a late invitation to the ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Cebu. Without ample time to prepare, it said it could only send its Manila-based defence attache.
“When that happened, I think the concern, especially on the part of the DFA, was, ‘We don’t want China not sending their premier. It would not look good on us as a host country,’” Lucio Pitlo, past president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies, said.

A12.text:
ASEAN summit: Who’s attending and what’s at stake?
Energy disruptions as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran is a key issue for the import-dependent bloc.
Southeast Asian countries that comprise the ASEAN economic bloc will meet in the Philippines this week as the region continues to bear the brunt of oil shortages caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as by US-China rivalry, which has hit economies hard.
The Manila summit will be held from November 15 to 17 and will include US President Donald Trump and several other world leaders.
The 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) aims to establish a single market, although it cannot impose decisions on members. It comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and East Timor, with a combined population of nearly 694 million, or 8.4 percent of the world’s population.
Several ASEAN meetings are held annually. This week’s summit is expected to be the final one for this year.
Beyond the energy crisis, other pressing issues include disputes over the South China Sea and trade.
Here’s what we know:
Who is attending?
In addition to leaders and representatives from the 11 member countries, other guests include:
- US President Donald Trump – Trump is expected to hold a special summit with ASEAN members on November 17 as Washington’s trade tensions with China continue. He is also set to hold a one-on-one meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Afterwards, Trump is due to head to China for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting on 18-19 November.
- India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi – Although India is not part of ASEAN, India is a key trading partner to member states.
- Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney – Carney is set to give a speech at the summit.
- Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva – His visit will be the first by a sitting Brazilian president to the Philippines. He is expected to discuss trade, defence and other areas of cooperation with ASEAN members.
- Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov – His visit comes after the Russia-ASEAN summit in July.
What are the key issues?
US-Iran war
The summit is being held at a time when Southeast Asian countries have been hit hard by shortages in oil and gas supplies from Middle Eastern suppliers amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
The Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia are among the most vulnerable to the energy disruptions in the Gulf, with Manila declaring a state of national energy emergency in March.
Millions of ASEAN citizens also live and work in the Middle East, where the war threatens their safety and earnings.
Meanwhile, Asian countries are worried the conflict could spill into the Strait of Malacca, a narrow waterway between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.
Trade
The US’s tariff war has seen ASEAN countries slapped with 10-12.5 percent tariff hikes since the beginning of US President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, prompting the bloc to strengthen trade relationships elsewhere.
South China Sea
China and four ASEAN members – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam – as well as Taiwan, have been locked in decades of territorial standoffs in the busy waterway.
The area is important as it is believed to host undersea deposits of oil and gas.
In 2005, the bloc began negotiating a “code of conduct” with China to discourage aggression and prevent major clashes. The negotiations have often stalled, however, partly due to flared tensions, especially between Manila and Beijing in recent years.
In 2023, the two sides agreed to speed things up and release a finished draft this year. At least 10 rounds of talks have been held this year, led by Malaysia, with a final round taking place in October.
However, analysts doubt a definite conclusion will be reached at the summit this week, meaning talks could continue into next year.
[truncated]

A22.text:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
Fighting escalates in Yemen’s Marib and al-Jawf, as UN migration agency says more than 340,000 Yemenis displaced since August.
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and five drones targeting different parts of the country, allegedly launched by the Iran-backed rebel group.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Security alert
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

A26.text:
Senior Hamas commander killed in Israeli strike in Gaza
By Nidal al-Mughrabi and Yomna Ehab
Nov 15 (Reuters) - Hamas said on Sunday that a senior commander who helped plan and oversee the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel had been killed in an Israeli airstrike, with the Israeli military confirming his death.
Samir Abu Younis, 53, the commander of the Rafah brigade, was killed on Saturday, said the Palestinian militant group's armed wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades.
The Israeli military said it had killed Abu Younis in a strike in the southern Gaza Strip overnight, adding that he had led the Rafah brigade since his predecessor, Nael Abu Obeid, was killed on September 15.
Medics said Abu Younis was killed and others were wounded in an airstrike that targeted him in a street in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip.
Hamas said Abu Younis joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and had held several senior operational roles in Rafah before becoming commander of the brigade.
His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.
An October 2025 ceasefire halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war but has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas' disarmament.
Gaza health authorities say atleast 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while 5 Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in the military campaign that Israel launched against Gaza after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in the October 7 attack.
(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi and Yomna Ehab; Additional reporting by Jana Choukeir; Editing by Nick Zieminski, Sanjeev Miglani, Rod Nickel and William Mallard)

A27.text:
Yemen government forces withdraw from area near Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Houthis in control
Nov 15 (Reuters) - Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognised Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
The government's retreat from the Bab el-Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime chokepoint, creating a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.
This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is one of the world's most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly from Asia to Europe via Egypt's Suez Canal.
The southern Yemeni forces said they were redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, including the capital Sanaa and Yemen's most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control.
"The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate," the southern forces said in a statement.
"This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats."
Government forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south in September in an attempt to seize control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el-Mandeb.
The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 UN-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key US ally and the world's biggest crude exporter.
Houthi attacks on the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the nine-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom's Red Sea oil export hub of Yanbu.
In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Fighting is intensifying around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to enter, and civilians are unable to leave.
(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari; Writing by Nayera Abdallah; Editing by William Mallard)

A31.text:
Netanyahu calls for Israeli unity government, Eisenkot dismisses 'tricks'
Israel's caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday reiterated his calls for a national unity government with his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who in turn dismissed the appeal as a ruse.
The latest exchange comes as Eisenkot is in the midst of negotiations to form a government, after he was tapped for the post of premier on Sunday.
A meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday "only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government" to guarantee Israel's security, Netanyahu said in a video statement, adding that such a government could "eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all".
He said this government would be made up of parties that recognise Israel "as a state for the Jewish people".
It would address security challenges, he added, most notably Iran which he claimed would "not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us".
The outgoing prime minister warned against Eisenkot's plan to form a minority government, presented as a "national emergency government".
Such a plan would see the 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot's bloc vote in favour of his government, against the 46 Netanyahu backers. The 26 other members of parliament, from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties, could abstain, allowing the government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset, which has 120 seats.
"Instead of trying to form a weak and dangerous government... let's meet in one room, without preconditions, put aside all our disagreements and all the boycotts, and reach agreements for the security and the future of the state," Netanyahu urged.
Minutes later, Eisenkot responded by saying Netanyahu "knows he lost the election", accusing him of playing "tricks" by appealing for a unity government.
"Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway; he claims to want unity but... sows division and stokes tensions as if there were no tomorrow," the former army chief said, adding that "these tricks don't work on me".
- 'Break with extremists' -
Eisenkot was tapped on Sunday to form a new government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.
Negotiations are expected to be difficult, especially as Netanyahu has waged a campaign to discredit Arab-Israeli parties, which gained a record number of seats in the election.
Netanyahu's proposed unity government would be made up of key Jewish parties ranging from the centre to the right, while excluding the Arab parties.
Eisenkot has indicated he would be open to forming a government with members of Netanyahu's Likud party, as well as outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism, provided their commitment to unity is "sincere".
But a unity government with Netanyahu himself remains unlikely, particularly after Eisenkot denounced his "racist" campaign against Arab parties on Friday.
Eisenkot on Saturday reiterated his calls for a "break with the extremists", notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir, as a condition for any participation in a government under his leadership.
Another point of contention is the election on Tuesday of the speaker of the Knesset, a post currently held by Amir Ohana, a close Netanyahu ally. The opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former officer in the Israeli army who was fifth on Gadi Eisenkot's list, to replace him.
"If they (Likud and its allies) are truly seeking a sincere political partnership, as they claim, they must allow the democratic process to unfold normally... and instruct their members of parliament to support the appointment of Matan Kahana," Eisenkot said.

A32.text:
Trump wagers time is on US side, for now, in dealing with Iran
The US can afford patience, but it should pair pressure with reassurance to its Middle Eastpartners.
US President Donald Trump has for now shelved negotiations for a nuclear agreement with Iran in favor of an economic strangulation strategy and naval embargo that is accelerating the country’s decline.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Friday “there’s no need for military action because we’ve weakened them so much,” adding that “victory is ensuring that they never have a nuclear weapon.”
In Trump’s calculation, time is on the US side, and he has a point. Iran has never been weaker. Its nuclear facilities, missile and drone bases, and military and naval forces have been bombed repeatedly. Its economy is in freefall, worsened by new sanctions on Iranian commercial banks. Oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are at pre-war levels, while Iran’s oil exports are shut down because of the US embargo and naval blockade. Iran’s top leaders know they could be targets in any further US or Israeli attacks.
Iran is resilient, but it is not winning, and it is not stronger than it was before the war. As an adversary, it is resourceful and relentless: it has mastered playing the weak hand, through proxy and drone warfare, calibrating its escalation with the US, and exploiting the vulnerabilities of neighbors who depend on the United States for protection. Iran’s people, meanwhile, are suffering more than ever from political oppression and economic strain.

A34.text:
US floated idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskiy says
By Olena Harmash
KYIV, Nov 14 (Reuters) - US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.
This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskiy said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?"he said.
"That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia's full-blown invasion in 2022.
Zelenskiy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.
'THIS WAR MUST BE ENDED FIRST'
Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskiy dismissed Russia's call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.
"We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first," he said.
US PresidentDonald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said on Saturday that the two sides had set out"maximalist positions" in the talks this week, but in private discussions both "understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war."
"Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions," Kushner said in a social media post.
Zelenskiy also dismissed Putin's suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow's inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.
"Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way," he said.
Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskiy said.
Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.
LARGE PRISONER EXCHANGE AGREED
The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskiy said.
The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.
Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskiy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.
"Putin personally does not support a ceasefire," he said.
Zelenskiy met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow. He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.
In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine's largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

A35.text:
Trump tells advisers he may hold off on Iran attacks barring new provocations, sources say
By Erin Banco, Humeyra Pamuk, Phil Stewart and Timour Azhari
WASHINGTON/RIYADH, Nov 14 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off onattacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
"I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.
The war has hiked global fuel prices and proven unpopular with US voters, who handed control of Congress to the Democrats in last week's midterm elections. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll taken shortly before the November 3 elections, 55% of Americans said the war was not worth the cost, and Vice President JD Vance cited it as the reason Trump's Republicans lost Congress.
Trump's private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.
"As Commander-in-Chief, President Trump is the architect and sole decision-maker who holds all the cards and will always ensure that America’s interests are protected," a White House official said in a statement. "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Only President Trump knows what he will do, and when."
The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment.
CALLS WITH SAUDI ARABIA AND TURKEY
In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way.
Trump told bin Salman on October 31 that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion.
Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has spoken withErdogan three times since October 28, according to Turkey's presidency. An official readout from the November 7 call stressed that tensions between Iran and the US need to end.
US intelligence agencies have assessed that the US naval blockade and economic sanctions are hurting the Iranian economy and would continue to put pressure on Tehran, two US officials briefed on the intelligence said.
Building on its months-long blockade of Iranian sea traffic, the US military is also seeking to prevent weapons and other sanctioned material from entering the country by land or through the Caspian Sea,Reuters first reported last week.
MILITARY OPTIONS
At the same time, the US military is ready to escalate if needed, three more people familiar with US planning said.
A third aircraft carrier is moving into the Middle East in the coming days to replace one of the two currently operating in the region, but all three carriers could stay if needed, the people said.

A36.text:
Analysis-A new 'Yalta'? Trump and Putin push for a meeting that Xi is wary of hosting
By Trevor Hunnicutt, Mei Mei Chu and Andrew Osborn
WASHINGTON/BEIJING/MOSCOW, Nov 14 (Reuters) - The world's three most powerful leaders could sit down together next week to discuss global flashpoints, from wars in Ukraine and Iran to nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence.
The prospects for any grand bargain emerging from the rare encounter, however, are slim.
Down-to-the-wire negotiations over a meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President XiJinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have not yet yielded an agenda or format fortalks, according to two people familiar with the planning. But a meeting is expected in Shenzhen, where the leaders will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, the people said.
The three men come with very different goals.
Putin sees a chance to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine on his terms. Trump — battered by his Republican Party's recent electoral losses — sees a moment for the history books, with possible movement toward a three-way agreement on nuclear arms control.
For Xi, however, it is an unpredictable gathering full of risks.
The Republican president's improvisational style clashes with Xi's scripted approach to high-profile events. And Trump's hope for arms control rubs against the reality that China — which has far fewer nuclear weapons than the US or Russia — considers itself a nuclear underdog.
"This is something the Chinese hate," said Edgard Kagan, a former senior Biden White House official for East Asia now with the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a think tank. "I think it’s fair to say the Chinese do not want arms control discussions with the United States. And they certainly don’t want to do it with the United States and Russia, because it suggests that they accept the framing that they are now a major nuclear power that should be subject to similar restrictions."
For smaller governmentsnot at the table, including Ukraine and Taiwan, the idea of the big powers possibly cutting a private deal without them is a cause of deep unease.
The meeting would be Trump’s latest in a series of diplomatic spectacles over his nearly six years as US president, including his prior meetings with Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. None of those meetings produced a breakthrough.
A senior Trump administration official said "we do not expect to get to any kind of agreement" on nuclear issuesbut added "it's time for China to sort of step up" and talk about the topic.
"China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state," said a spokesperson for Beijing's embassy in Washington on Friday. "We have nothing to share at the moment."
Russia's embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
SOME NATIONS FEAR A NEW 'YALTA' CONFERENCE
The proposed meeting has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
For Russian nationalists, the prospect of an updated version of Yalta has generated excitement, potentially opening the door to an agreement to end thefour-year-old Ukraine conflict in a manner that would favor Moscow.
Just holding the meeting elevates Russia to the status of a superpower alongside China and the US, they say.
“It shows who is important in the world: We are, China and the West," Russian nationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin told Radio Sputnik this week. "It’s deeply symbolic — it’s a confirmation of a multi-polar world that the West denies.”
But the possible meeting has generated anxiety from Kyiv to Tokyo, according to people briefed on those governments' reactions.

A369.text:
Yemen government forces withdraw from area near Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Houthis in control
Nov 15 - Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognised Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
The government's retreat from the Bab el-Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime chokepoint, creating a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.
This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is one of the world's most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly from Asia to Europe via Egypt's Suez Canal.
The southern Yemeni forces said they were redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, including the capital Sanaa and Yemen's most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control.
"The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate," the southern forces said in a statement.
"This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats."
Government forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south in September in an attempt to seize control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el-Mandeb.
The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 UN-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key US ally and the world's biggest crude exporter.
Houthi attacks on the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the nine-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom's Red Sea oil export hub of Yanbu.
In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Fighting is intensifying around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to enter, and civilians are unable to leave. REUTERS

A38.text:
STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.
Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.
Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.
We are dazzled
This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.
Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.
It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.
Nevertheless, it happened.
Rapid reuse is firmly on the horizon
Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

A4.text:
Iran says it targets US radar in Bahrain. What do we know?
The Bahrain Defence Force says its air defence systems thwart several Iranian ‘aerial attacks’.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base in response to what it describes as hostile US actions.
Sirens sounded in Bahrain on Sunday as its Ministry of Interior urged residents to “remain calm” and “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It was the second time in three days that the IRGC claimed to have targeted a US radar system in Bahrain.
The US military said it intercepted two Iranian drones on Friday but has yet to comment on Sunday’s claim.
Here is what we know:
What happened on Sunday?
The IRGC said it struck the radar at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base, according to a statement carried by the IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts within about three hours, the first about 4:30am (01:30 GMT). The ministry warned of a “potential threat” and urged residents to seek shelter. It gave no further details about the threat.
The Bahrain Defence Force also said its air defence systems thwarted several Iranian “aerial attacks” targeting the kingdom.
In its statement, the IRGC said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed and claimed that US efforts to escort ships through the waterway had failed. It warned that any US attack would draw a more severe response.
What happened in Bahrain on Friday?
The IRGC said on Friday that it destroyed a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, saying it had shot down two IRGC drones and there were no injuries or damage.
In a statement carried by Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim News Agency, the IRGC called the operation a “serious warning” over what it described as aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that Friday marked the first time since early September that Iran had claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.
Tehran has told the United Nations Security Council it would respond immediately to renewed US or Israeli attacks and has accused Bahrain and other Gulf states of supporting US military operations. Bahrain has called for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and other countries in the region and demanded they stop.
Manama, Bahrain, is where the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet is based. A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks had damaged or destroyed buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
What has happened in the Strait of Hormuz?
The IRGC’s navy said two oil tankers struck sea mines on Saturday while trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iran’s state news agency IRNA, it said the vessels had switched off their navigation and tracking systems and were using what it called an “unauthorised” route.
The IRGC said two other tankers turned back towards the Gulf after receiving warnings from its maritime traffic control centre.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Mohammed Vall said on Saturday that there were “two similar incidents yesterday” and the number of tankers hitting mines has increased.
Vall said Iran claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under its “full control” and “only Iran and Oman have the right to control it”. The United States rejects that claim.
According to Vall, Iran blamed the incidents on the tanker owners and the countries backing them, saying they had failed to comply with the regulations Iran imposed on passage through the strait.

A41.text:
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
- Published
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
[truncated]

A418.text:
The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.
The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.
“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”
ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.
“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.
Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.
“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.
For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017.
[truncated]

A42.text:
Copper wire upgrade behind US flight suspension, transport secretary says
- Published
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said.
Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment.
Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights.
Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment.
Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said.
The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued."
The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes, prompting the shutdown on safety grounds.
The government was now trying to understand whether the root cause was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.
The four-hour suspension from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US.
More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled that day, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers, with more than 5,900 cancelled and 7,000 delayed on Saturday.
In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the US flight schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday.
US officials have said they did not believe the issue was as a result of a cyber-attack or a rogue AI agent, though Duffy said an investigation into the exact cause was under way.
Bryan Bedford, who heads the FAA, told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related."
L3Harris said on Saturday that it had completed more than 70% of the work it had been tasked to undertake to modernise US air traffic communications infrastructure before the shutdown.
The company said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation, adding: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn (£22.8bn) for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.
Duffy previously said the system needed a $50bn overhaul.
Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"
A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.
A failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system in 2023 prompted a grounding that lasted an hour and 52 minutes, delaying about 9,500 flights and cancelling about 1,300.

A46.text:
Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
- Published
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.
Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.
A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".
Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.
The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.
Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".
It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."
Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".
It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".
Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.
He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.
The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.

A49.text:
Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
- Published
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta, which also runs WhatsApp and Instagram, 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech company.
A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.
The charge is related to a feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.
Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. A preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery, according to the Italian regulator.
The regulator said it had taken into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact that the feature was "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation" in its decision.
Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine.
"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."
Last month, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

A5.text:
What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now know
US officials say a routine upgrade that went awry caused the mass disruption of air travel.
Airlines are still scrambling to return operations to normal after the longest and only second nationwide stop of flights in the United States since the attacks of 9/11 in 2001.
More than 5,000 flights were cancelled in the US on Saturday after over 9,000 were scrapped a day earlier as the knock-on effects continued from Friday’s abrupt ground stop. The stoppage was halted after more than four hours on Friday night, but airports and carriers were still grappling with large backlogs and resulting delays.
The decision to suddenly ground all planes on Friday initially triggered speculation of a cyberattack.
But officials have since ruled that out and named the reason for the weekend disruptions as a routine replacement of the communications routers that connect the US air traffic control system.
Here’s everything we know about what went wrong:
What happened?
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop of flights at 3:54pm East Coast time (20:54 GMT) on Friday, citing a telecommunications outage affecting air route traffic control centres.
The outage caused thousands of flights to be cancelled or delayed across the US.
The ground stop was removed at 8:15pm on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday), but hundreds of flights were still delayed or cancelled that night, according to the aviation analytics firm Cirium.
Aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land during the ground stop while international flights were handled on a case-by-case basis with some allowed to depart despite the restrictions.
What caused the ground stop?
A routine upgrade was being carried out – maintenance work that ultimately overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop, US officials said.
L3Harris, a contractor, was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fibre optic lines in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.
The router in that location then started overloading the air traffic control system, causing communications disruptions. When officials couldn’t locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.
“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” Duffy said.
The transportation secretary said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router to start flooding other ones.
“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters.
The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en route centres.
The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS), a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two routers that were updated on Friday. An official told the Reuters news agency it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas.
An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.
Ageing technology and equipment alongside a shortage of several thousand controllers have long been concerns plaguing the US air traffic control system.
Duffy on Friday called for $50bn in funding to upgrade these systems, up from his earlier request of $30bn after Congress approved $12.5bn last year.
So it wasn’t a cyberattack?
No.
White House officials had convened an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday amid concerns that the incident was due to a cyberattack. But the US government has since said it did not believe that was the cause.
“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said.
[truncated]

A53.text:
'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.
"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

A57.text:
How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
- Published
An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.
Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday.
US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.
Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
What caused the stoppage?
On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network.
As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.
According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.
As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.
This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.
As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."
Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.
In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage.
He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day.
In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation.
"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said.
Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel.
"You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said
"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.
A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".
He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.

A58.text:
World
SpaceX Starship successfully re-docks at Texas launch pad after orbiting Earth
Company hopes accomplishment will further efforts to create fully reusable rocket
SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.
"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. "Look at her! Baby, she's back!"
Calling it an "epic day," Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. "Looks great," he reported via X.
SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. "Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)."
The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 124-metre behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
Starship continued circling the world 265 kilometres up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.
It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.
Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe as part of efforts to end Russia's war in Ukraine, warning that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent's borders.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian oil facility supporting Moscow's war effort, Ukraine's General Staff said in a statement on Saturday.
"In my view, this can be dangerous," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday, referring to the new security framework. "This should not be the main agenda." His comments were embargoed until Saturday.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."
European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent's security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate the future of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

Mientras corre el plazo de 28 días otorgado por el presidente Isaac Herzog para formar gobierno en Israel, donde el bloque opositor busca articular un gabinete minoritario con respaldo de partidos de base árabe, el primer ministro Benjamin Netanyahu instó este sábado a su rival político Gadi Eisenkot a negociar una gestión de "unidad nacional" y "sin condiciones" pero la propuesta fue rechazada de plano.
A través de un video que difundió esta tarde en sus rede sociales, el primer ministro en funciones reveló que en una charla que mantuvo el jueves le pidió al líder opositor -encargado de formar Ejecutivo tras las elecciones de octubre- excluir a los partidos árabes ante la amenaza nuclear de Irán.
"El régimen iraní, que aspira a la destrucción de Israel, vuelve a actuar para reactivar su programa nuclear", alertó en su mensaje Netanyahu.
En ese marco, instó este sábado a Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar), a conformar un "gobierno de unidad nacional" integrado exclusivamente por todos los partidos de mayoría judía porque alertó que un Ejecutivo que dependa del respaldo de las fuerzas árabes no estará en condiciones de hacer frente a la amenaza iraní.
A diferencia de llamados anteriores, Netanyahu evitó especificar esta vez que él deba encabezar dicha coalición. Y, aseguró que la sesión informativa sobre seguridad que mantuvo el jueves con Eisenkot "no hizo más que reforzar mi convicción de lo imprescindible que resulta formar en este momento un gobierno de unidad nacional; un gobierno que incluya a todos los partidos que apoyan la existencia de Israel como el Estado del pueblo judío".

La respuesta de Eisenkot: "Una enésima maniobra propagandística"
El líder de Yashar! respondió velozmente a la propuesta de Netanyahu y la rechazó de plano, calificándola como "una enésima maniobra propagandística", según declaraciones citadas por el diario The Times of Israel.
Eisenkot señaló además que los equipos negociadores del Likud y de Yashar ya tenían programada una reunión para este domingo.
"Dice querer la unidad, pero al mismo tiempo degrada una ceremonia institucional en la Knéset, sembrando división e incitando al odio como si no hubiera un mañana", advirtió Eisenkot en referencia a la controversia suscitada por la retirada de legisladores durante la entonación del himno Hatikvá en la apertura parlamentaria, episodio que Netanyahu mencionó en su video.
Y concluyó: "Buen intento, pero conmigo no funcionan estos trucos. Y tampoco funcionan con los ciudadanos de Israel".
Claves del llamado y la amenaza iraní
Netanyahu justificó su convocatoria "sin condiciones previas" en informes sobre la reactivación del programa atómico de Teherán y advirtió que el régimen iraní no dudaría en emplear armas nucleares contra Israel en cuanto logre retomar el enriquecimiento de uranio.
En este marco, reivindicó operaciones militares previas como "León Rampante" y "Rugido del León" para neutralizar amenazas existenciales, y propuso abordar dentro de una coalición amplia la controversia por el reclutamiento militar de los ultraortodoxos (haredíes).
La situación política en Israeal se complicó tras las elecciones parlamentarias del 27 de octubre que dejaron a la Knéset de 120 escaños fragmentada y sin mayoría automática para los bloques tradicionales.
Desde entonces, el bloque de Netanyahu, el Likud y sus aliados religiosos y de extrema derecha suman 53 escaños (27 del Likud), perdiendo la mayoría que sostuvieron durante los últimos cuatro años.

La Casa Blanca confirmó la celebración de una cumbre inédita entre Donald Trump, Xi Jinping y Vladimir Putin el próximo jueves en China, en la que abordarán la guerra en Oriente Medio pero, afirman, dejarán fuera el conflicto en Ucrania.
El encuentro entre los líderes de Estados Unidos, China y Rusia, del que se venía especulando desde hace semanas, se llevará a cabo finalmente al margen del Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC) en Shenzhen, en el sur chino.
Moscú también confirmó la reunión. "Se ha alcanzado un acuerdo para la celebración, el día 19, de una reunión trilateral entre los presidentes Putin, Xi y Trump. Ese encuentro tendrá lugar en Shenzhen en el marco de la cumbre de la APEC", dijo el portavoz de la Presidencia rusa, Dmitri Peskov, a la agencia Interfax.
El evento marcará un nuevo paso en el regreso a la escena internacional de Putin, aislado por Occidente desde la invasión de Ucrania en 2022, poco más de un año después de su reunión con Trump en Alaska.
A los líderes de estas tres potencias nucleares no les faltarán temas sobre la mesa durante una cumbre que promete dejar una foto histórica, aunque los expertos ven poco probable que arroje resultados concretos.
"El presidente ha dejado claro que, entre otros temas, discutirá la reducción del arsenal de armas nucleares en el mundo. El presidente cree que esta proliferación es muy peligrosa", declaró el viernes por la noche a la prensa Olivia Wales, portavoz de la Casa Blanca.
"Creo que el presidente sí tiene intención de hablar sobre Irán en la reunión trilateral con Xi Jinping y Vladimir Putin", añadió un funcionario estadounidense, que habló bajo condición de anonimato.
Pero Washington tiene "otra vía" de negociaciones con Kiev y Moscú, añadió.
"China no forma realmente parte de esa vía, así que no parece apropiado abordar allí la cuestión de Ucrania", agregó, en referencia a las conversaciones que enviados estadounidenses han mantenido en los últimos días con Putin y el presidente ucraniano, Volodimir Zelenski.
Esta declaración demuestra la voluntad de mantener la cuestión ucraniana en el marco de las conversaciones con Kiev y Moscú que se reanudaron esta semana y en las que los europeos esperan participar.
Tras las negociaciones ruso-ucranianas celebradas en Abu Dhabi bajo mediación estadounidense, Washington aseguró contar con el visto bueno de Moscú para sumar a los europeos a la mesa.
Reunidos el viernes en una cumbre en Dublín, los líderes europeos acordaron acudir representados por cinco países (Francia, Alemania, Reino Unido, Polonia e Italia) y por delegados de la Unión Europea.
"Por primera vez, en las próximas semanas habrá conversaciones de paz concretas en las que los europeos estarán representados", celebró el canciller alemán, Friedrich Merz, quien lanzó una advertencia a Estados Unidos antes del viaje de Trump a Shenzhen: "Por favor, nada de sorpresas".
¿Una nueva Yalta?
The Wall Street Journal reveló a mediados de octubre la idea de esta cumbre trilateral. Según el diario, fue el propio Putin quien, en pleno acercamiento con Trump, propuso el encuentro a sus homólogos para negociar el fin del conflicto en Ucrania, sin la presencia de Kiev ni de los europeos.
Esa posibilidad despertó el temor a que Washington, Beijing y Moscú cedieran a la tentación de repartirse el mundo en una nueva Yalta, en alusión a la histórica conferencia de febrero de 1945 entre el estadounidense Franklin D. Roosevelt, el británico Winston Churchill y el soviético Iósif Stalin.
Tampoco está previsto que Trump se reúna a solas con Putin, a diferencia de Xi, con quien almorzará el jueves.
Será su cuarto cara a cara desde que el republicano regresó a la Casa Blanca en enero de 2025, en un encuentro que previsiblemente tendrá a la inteligencia artificial como eje central.
"La situación de Nvidia no debería tener incidencia en el viaje", aseguró otro funcionario estadounidense bajo condición de anonimato.
