Iran claims attack on US military airbase in Bahrain
Iranian military confirmed on Sunday an attack on a US military base in Bahrain, in its second targeting the Middle Eastern country in the space of three days. Bahrain's military said it had intercepted several Iranian attacks, with the foreign ministry confirming its air defence systems had shot down Iranian drones, preventing them from reaching their intended targets.
Blasts rang out over Bahrain early on Sunday as Iran's Guards said they attacked a US military base in the Gulf nation, which has been heavily targeted during the Middle East war.
Sirens sounded and authorities posted several alerts on social media urging residents to seek shelter, their first warnings since September.
After a lull in attacks Bahrain, which hosts a major US naval base, has been targeted twice in three days. The energy-rich Gulf has borne the brunt of Iranian strikes during the war.
Bahrain's military said it intercepted several Iranian attacks, "preventing them from reaching their intended targets". The foreign ministry said air defence systems shot down Iranian drones.
Explosions could be heard around 4am (0100 GMT), an AFP journalist said, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30 am.
The interior ministry, posting on X, called on "residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels".

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their forces carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a base, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster.
"The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the Guards said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response," it added.
During more than eight months of war, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz oil trade route and struck infrastructure including airports, seaports, energy facilities, and US assets across the region.

'Settling scores'
Bahrain is among the Gulf countries that have weathered thousands of Iranian drone and missile strikes since the war began on February 28.
The tiny island nation "rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences", the foreign ministry statement said.
On Friday, the Revolutionary Guards said their forces targeted a US early warning radar system in Bahrain – the first strike against a Gulf country since early September.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said it shot down two Iranian drones targeting the Gulf island, reporting no casualties or damage in the attack.
CENTCOM, which oversees American military operations in the region, said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil since the summer via Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump, whose steep reverse in midterm elections was partly blamed on the Iran war, plans to discuss the conflict at a trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts this week, an official said Friday.
Months of diplomacy have failed to resolve the war, which began with surprise US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Netanyahu renews call for Israeli unity government as Eisenkot dismisses 'tricks'
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday renewed his call for a national unity government with Gadi Eisenkot, who dismissed the appeal as a political ploy. This comes as the incoming premier is in the midst of negotiations to form a new administration.
Israel's caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday reiterated his calls for a national unity government with his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who in turn dismissed the appeal as a ruse.
The latest exchange comes as Eisenkot is in the midst of negotiations to form a government, after he was tapped for the post of premier on Sunday.
Read moreIsrael's new parliament to be sworn in as Eisenkot prepares government
A meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday "only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government" to guarantee Israel's security, Netanyahu said in a video statement, adding that such a government could "eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all".
He said this government would be made up of parties that recognise Israel "as a state for the Jewish people".
It would address security challenges, he added, most notably Iran which he claimed would "not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us".
The outgoing prime minister warned against Eisenkot's plan to form a minority government, presented as a "national emergency government".
Such a plan would see the 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot's bloc vote in favour of his government, against the 46 Netanyahu backers. The 26 other members of parliament, from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties, could abstain, allowing the government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset, which has 120 seats.
"Instead of trying to form a weak and dangerous government... let's meet in one room, without preconditions, put aside all our disagreements and all the boycotts, and reach agreements for the security and the future of the state," Netanyahu urged.
Minutes later, Eisenkot responded by saying Netanyahu "knows he lost the election", accusing him of playing "tricks" by appealing for a unity government.
"Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway; he claims to want unity but... sows division and stokes tensions as if there were no tomorrow," the former army chief said, adding that "these tricks don't work on me".
'Break with extremists'
Eisenkot was tapped on Sunday to form a new government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.
Negotiations are expected to be difficult, especially as Netanyahu has waged a campaign to discredit Arab-Israeli parties, which gained a record number of seats in the election.
Netanyahu's proposed unity government would be made up of key Jewish parties ranging from the centre to the right, while excluding the Arab parties.
Read moreEisenkot pushes October 7 inquiry as Netanyahu targets Arab parties in tense new parliament
Eisenkot has indicated he would be open to forming a government with members of Netanyahu's Likud party, as well as outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism, provided their commitment to unity is "sincere".
But a unity government with Netanyahu himself remains unlikely, particularly after Eisenkot denounced his "racist" campaign against Arab parties on Friday.
Eisenkot on Saturday reiterated his calls for a "break with the extremists", notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir, as a condition for any participation in a government under his leadership.
Another point of contention is the election on Tuesday of the speaker of the Knesset, a post currently held by Amir Ohana, a close Netanyahu ally. The opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former officer in the Israeli army who was fifth on Gadi Eisenkot's list, to replace him.

U.S. negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine’s potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.
This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelensky said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday.
“The Americans raised a question: ’What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’” he said.
“That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation.”
Kyiv Independent editor on the challenges of reporting a war without an end
Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.
Zelensky reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.
‘This war must be ended first’
Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelensky dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.
“We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.
Zelensky also dismissed Putin’s suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow’s inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.
“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” he said.
Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelensky said.
Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.
Large prisoner exchange agreed
The two days of U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelensky said.
The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.
Russia and Ukraine agree to large-scale prisoner swap as talks conclude with no major breakthrough
U.S. peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelensy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.
“Putin personally does not support a ceasefire,” he said.

A227.text:

During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

A228.text:
MANILA, Philippines – Police clashed with protesters at Liwasang Bonifacio on Sunday morning, November 15, as activists opposing Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump tried to march toward the ASEAN Summit venue.
The protesters were trying to reach the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), the venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Police blocked the protesters from proceeding to the summit venue. Some of the protesters managed to slip through several layers of policemen armed with shields. The cops, however, managed to block the protesters again.
Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) President Jerome Adonis said police told them they could not hold a street protest because they did not have a permit.
After nearly an hour of attempts to march to PICC, the protesters retreated to Liwasang Bonifacio. Despite this, at least 11 protesters were arrested by police within freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines.
Ines said at least 16 personnel from the Manila Police District were injured.
Cops dragged protesters into a police vehicle. Some officers were seen slapping, kicking, and punching one activist as they took him away.
Adonis questioned the legality of the arrests, saying they were made inside a freedom park.
“Ang gulo ho nanggaling sa pulis. Hindi po galing sa amin. Nagdedepensa lang kami ng hanay namin,” he added. (The trouble started with the police, not us. We were only defending our ranks.)
Rappler asked the Manila Police District why the protesters were arrested, but it had yet to respond as of writing.
Under the Revised Penal Code, a person arrested without a warrant should be brought to court within a maximum of 36 hours, and that is for grave violations.
Police also towed the truck that protesters had used as a makeshift stage. Adonis accused police of puncturing their vehicles with nails.
In Liwasang Bonifacio, where the protesters plan to camp out, human manure was scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, the “father of the Philippine revolution.”
Bayan Muna Chairperson Teddy Casiño, who was also at the protest, claimed that the police were behind this.
“Isang malaking ka-hipokrituhan ang ginagawa ng gobyerno. Nagpapakita ng hospitality sa mga dayuhan pero binabastos ang kanyang mga mamamayan,” Casiño said. (The government’s actions are widely hypocritical. It shows hospitality to foreign visitors while disrespecting its own people.)
Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service later cleaned the human manure.
Concerns over Pax Silica
Protesters have raised concerns that Pax Silica could displace Indigenous peoples and farming communities in the planned 4,000-acre industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.
Pax Silica is a US-led initiative that seeks to strengthen supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries. The signing of the Pax Silica agreement had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.
Trump is expected to arrive in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for the Special ASEAN-US Summit.
However, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified that the Philippines would not sign the agreement during the 49th ASEAN Summit.
“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters on Tuesday, November 10.
Despite the delay, the Philippines eyes to sign the deal with the US before the year ends, Rodolfo said.
Amid the protests, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the public to reconsider holding demonstrations during the summit.
“Whatever their demands may be, I hope these are not pursued through protests, although I recognize that this is their right.
[truncated]

A374.text:
Bahrain intercepts Iranian aerial attacks as Tehran says it attacked US base
- Bahrain said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks after warnings told residents to seek shelter.

AI generated
Bahrain intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks, it said on Nov 15, while Tehran said it had struck a US military base in the Gulf country amid uncertainty over a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The first such interceptions by Bahraini air defences since September followed two warnings of potential threats, urging residents to seek shelter.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked a US military base in Bahrain in retaliation for “hostile US actions”, Iran’s Fars news agency reported.
The Bahraini military said its air defences had intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, accusing Tehran of continuing its “systematic hostile approach” towards the kingdom.

Two days earlier, the Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain. The US military denied this, saying it had intercepted two Iranian drones without any damage.
Diplomatic efforts to end the almost nine-month conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough, with sporadic attacks continuing despite a broader lull in fighting between the US and Iran.
The war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28 and subsequently spread across the region, with Tehran launching missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf countries.
President Donald Trump has said in recent days that he might hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, but that he would maintain a US naval blockade, Reuters reported on Nov 14.

Senior Hamas commander killed in Israeli strike in Gaza

A393.text:
US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
WASHINGTON, Nov 14 - A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that has disrupted more than 20,000 flights since Friday may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris, government officials said Saturday.
The incident is the latest painful example of the aging US air traffic control telecom system and the struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working.
The FAA's aging telecom systems in recent years have failed after errant fiber cuts, accidental deletion of files and a strong chemical smell caused by a melted component. The system will fail again until it is properly upgraded, officials said.
"This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.
Duffy said on Friday L3Harris was conducting routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber at at least one remote location. Officials told Reuters there may have been problems with routers installed in both Arkansas and Texas.
"We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said.
L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and was "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel."
L3 noted it has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.
The FAA spends $1 billion annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with more modern fiber-based communications.
"We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Duffy said, noting that "virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital."
The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers across the country, which prompted the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop because it could not identify a root cause.
Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities.
Bedford said the FAA had to take the action when it lost "the ability for those routers to communicate data." The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong.
The FAA said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at the centers. It did not lead to centers going dark. The routers being replaced are about 25 years old, Duffy said, and were supposed to be replaced in 2006.
NOT THE FIRST TIME
Small mishaps leading to catastrophic consequences are not new to the US air traffic control network. A 2023 FAA nationwide ground stop that lasted 90 minutes and disrupted 11,000 flights was caused by a government contractor unintentionally deleting files.
That led to the first nationwide ground stop since the hijacked airplane attacks on September 11, 2001.
Friday's outage hit as a surge in travelers began weekend travel. Noting the poor timing, Duffy said they would reevaluate when work is done at smaller facilities to prevent future disruptions.
The FAA got $12.5 billion to upgrade its badly aging air traffic control and telecom system from Congress and Duffy has asked for $50 billion more for air traffic control and airports.
The FAA only last week said it would replace by the end of 2028 outdated floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities.
The FAA relies on a telecoms system it is racing to replace as well as decades-old Compaq computers and replacement parts bought on eBay.
[truncated]

A396.text:
SpaceX’s Starship set for return to Earth after booster catch aborted
- SpaceX’s Starship was healthy in orbit and due to return to Starbase on Nov 14. It was the 15th test flight, aimed at a first “catch” of the ship and booster.
- The Super Heavy booster aborted its capture after a GNC issue and self-destructed over the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX called it a “mixed bag”, but Starship still reached orbit and launched 26 Starlink satellites.
- The failed catch shows the risk of SpaceX’s reusable rocket plan, which NASA also needs for Artemis. SpaceX says Starship must pass many checks, and fuel transfer in orbit is still unsolved.
AI generated
STARBASE, Texas - SpaceX said its Starship spacecraft was “healthy” as it orbited the Earth and on track to return on Nov 14 to its Texas launch site, where Elon Musk’s company was planning to “catch” the vehicle for the first time.
It was the 15th test flight of the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket system, originally meant to feature a groundbreaking twin capture of both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship.
Successful recoveries of both stages would have marked a milestone in the space industry’s decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems that can drastically reduce mission costs and make frequent launches possible.
But that achievement slipped out of reach minutes after the 124m rocket blasted off on Nov 13 from its launch pad at Starbase.
After the mid-air separation of the two stages, the Super Heavy booster was descending when its guidance, navigation and control system aborted the capture attempt.
“The booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with the catch,” SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said, adding that engineers were still investigating the root cause.
Super Heavy, which SpaceX had caught three times previously, diverted to the Gulf of Mexico just off the launch site. It automatically self-destructed – a fireball erupting from the booster – before hitting the water.
The Starship spacecraft that gives the rocket system its name was, meanwhile, orbiting Earth, which it was expected to do 14 times before returning on Nov 14 at the end of a 22-hour flight.
It successfully deployed 26 satellites shortly after arriving in space Friday to join Musk’s Starlink satellite internet constellation.
“Overall the ship’s still looking healthy, and we are still on track for a catch attempt here at Starbase,” Huot said on Nov 14.
Flight control will make a decision on whether to proceed with the capture attempt about two hours before its scheduled return at 3.18pm (5.18am on Nov 15, Singapore time).
“If you want to get back to the east coast of Texas, you have to fly over the entire continent to get back there. So inevitably, you’re flying over land and we spend a lot of time figuring out the safest way to do that,” senior SpaceX engineer Lars Blackmore said.
“Once the rocket is flying over land, there’s 21 minutes where the operators can’t do anything, and so we’re just going to be holding our breath for that time.”
The return path will see Starship fly over lightly inhabited desert areas, weave over towns and then carry out a “giant swoosh manoeuvre” in its final approach, looping around the cities of Texas’ Rio Grande Valley and approaching its landing site from the east.
Complex catch
The “catch” of Starship is extraordinarily complex because the spaceship will be falling much faster and from a much higher altitude than the booster.
Like the three previous Super Heavy recoveries, Starship is meant to carry out a controlled descent and nestle vertically between two mechanical “chopstick arms” at the launch site.
Some versions of the Starship spacecraft are designed to launch internet satellites and data centres into orbit, while other iterations will be made to ferry people to the Moon and Mars.
[truncated]

LONDON – Chips do not stop shipping because a chief executive leaves, so Nvidia will continue to be a key global player in its industrial sector. Still, what Jensen Huang took with him when he left Nvidia were his unique business acumen and priceless political connections. And both are irreplaceable.

A409.text:
US proposes Ukraine cede territory in exchange for joining NATO: Zelensky
- The US reportedly suggested Ukraine cede Donbas for NATO entry, Zelensky said. He said this was the first time such a demand was raised.
- Talks in Abu Dhabi ended without a breakthrough. All sides agreed European officials should join future negotiations.
- Zelensky said Russia rejected an energy ceasefire and called Putin’s wider security demands “dangerous”, warning they could trigger more wars.
AI generated
KYIV – Washington suggested Kyiv cede land to Moscow in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released on Nov 14, saying his country’s relationship with the Western alliance is “back on the agenda.”
Zelensky also warned of the dangers of Moscow’s push to redraw “influence” in Europe and said the Kremlin was “betting everything” on this winter’s military campaign.
Moscow has pounded Ukraine in the run-up to winter, with Russian President Vladimir Putin showing no sign of backing down.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met both Putin and Zelensky Nov 12 after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, which ended with no breakthrough.
Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.
In Dublin on Nov 13, Europe chose five countries – France, Germany, Italy, the UK and Poland – to send representatives to the talks.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said, adding:
“After providing Ukraine with this kind of defence support, seeing this kind of development of our army and this strength in our defence, they cannot simply let Ukraine go.”
He said the discussion showed that “NATO is back on the agenda” for Ukraine.
NATO and Washington have not yet commented.
Russia meanwhile continued its bombardment on Nov 14, with deadly strikes in the eastern city of Pavlohrad and in a village near Zaporizhzhia, which is now just a few dozen kilometres from the front line.
Kyiv seeks guarantees
Zelensky said Kyiv was discussing security guarantees with Western partners and that Ukrainians would ultimately decide whether to accept any deal.
He insisted Ukraine would not recognise any land seized by Moscow’s troops as Russian.
Russia has consistently said Kyiv joining NATO is a red line and in 2022 launched its invasion, saying the West planned to incorporate Ukraine into the alliance.
The Kremlin has also ruled out foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine and wider ceasefires.
But Putin earlier this week proposed a “humanitarian” mission to the eastern town of Kostyantynivka, which Moscow announced it had seized in the summer but where Kyiv says fighting continues.
Zelensky said the proposal was a bid to advance Russian gains in Donetsk. “Their next steps will be our other cities in Donbas,” he said.
Moscow’s troops have inched westwards but have been unable to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.
‘First, end the war’
Russia has tried to reframe negotiations on ending the war – Europe’s worst since World War II – into a conversation on the continent’s wider security.
In 2021, before its Ukraine invasion, Moscow issued an ultimatum to the West to pull back NATO troops from eastern Europe.
Moscow’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, this week called for a “new, modern Yalta”, drawing criticism from European leaders.
Zelensky warned that any discussion of wider security arrangements should come only after the war has ended.
European leaders have reacted coolly to the proposal for a new security architecture.
“We do not need to discuss that, it already exists,” Germany’s Friedrich Merz said Nov 13.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Nov 14 that “those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it” and, by extension, all of Europe.
“That is the spirit of defeat. That is a recipe for another war.
[truncated]

A410.text:
Trump tells advisers he may hold off on Iran attacks barring new provocations, sources say
- Trump may delay attacks on Iran if Tehran and the Houthis avoid new provocations, after advice from advisers, intelligence briefings, and calls with Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
- The war has raised fuel prices and angered US voters, with 55% saying it was not worth the cost, helping Democrats win Congress, Reuters/Ipsos found.
- The US military still has escalation plans, including a third aircraft carrier and possible strikes on nuclear sites, while Israel keeps pressing for more action.
AI generated
WASHINGTON/RIYADH — US President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
“I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly,” Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Nov 12.
The war has hiked global fuel prices and proven unpopular with US voters, who handed control of Congress to the Democrats in last week's midterm elections. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll taken shortly before the Nov 3 elections, 55% of Americans said the war was not worth the cost, and Vice-President J.D. Vance cited it as the reason Trump's Republicans lost Congress.
Trump’s private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.
“As Commander-in-Chief, President Trump is the architect and sole decision-maker who holds all the cards and will always ensure that America’s interests are protected,” a White House official said in a statement.
“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Only President Trump knows what he will do, and when.”
The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment.
Calls with Saudi Arabia and Turkey
In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way.
Trump told bin Salman on Oct 31 that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has spoken with Erdogan three times since Oct 28, according to Turkey’s presidency. An official readout from the Nov 7 call stressed that tensions between Iran and the US need to end.
US intelligence agencies have assessed that the US naval blockade and economic sanctions are hurting the Iranian economy and would continue to put pressure on Tehran, two US officials briefed on the intelligence said.
Building on its months-long blockade of Iranian sea traffic, the US military is also seeking to prevent weapons and other sanctioned material from entering the country by land or through the Caspian Sea, Reuters first reported last week.
[truncated]

A417.text:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.
Iran has targeted an airbase inBahrainin the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.
According to Iranian media, the IRGC said it had sent six drones to attack a US radar system hosted in the US-allied island state.
Explosions were heard around the capital, Manama, but Bahrain authorities say their air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets.
Bahrain, which lies directly across the Persian Gulf from Iran, is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, and has been repeatedly attacked by Tehran during the course of the war, which has seen flare-ups in strikes amid long bouts of inaction.
There are fears Iran’s attacks this morning might signal a resumption of the war while US President Donald Trump has threatened but refrained from returning to major combat. Negotiations to end the war remain at a stalemate, with the US maintaining its naval blockade and Iran its stranglehold over the strait of Hormuz.
Developments in the Red Sea this morning will add to further concerns for Gulf oil flows.
The Yemeni government forces supported by Saudi Arabia, fighting the Houthis, have retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb area, giving the Iran-aligned rebels even greater control over the critical shipping lane, which Saudi Arabia and other Gulf oil producers had been relying on to get their supplies out.
Elsewhere, Hamas has confirmed that a senior commander involved in planning the 7 October attacks was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday.
Bahrain locals: 'I was hoping this period was behind us'
After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.
Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.
It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.
Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:
I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.
They said they had attacked the air base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. The base is about a 30-minute drive south of Manama.
US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes.
Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.
The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.
That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.
Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.

A420.text:
Italy’s data protection agency has fined Facebook parent company Meta €805m ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their specific consent.
Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement.
Meta said it would appeal the decision. A company spokesperson said “we strongly disagree” with the assessment by the regulators “and the disproportionate level of the fine”.
In late October, authorities in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn for misleading the state’s residents for more than a decade about the use of their data – a record fine for the company, which slammed it as a “tax” on freedom of expression.
Saturday’s latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech company.
In 2021, Amazon received a more than €1.1bn fine for breaching competition law.
That sum was subsequently reduced to €752m on appeal.
The Italian penalty imposed on Facebook relates to its gallery suggestions feature, available since 2023, which suggests photos and videos from a user’s phone gallery as ideas for posts as they are browsing.
According to Italy’s regulator, Facebook requested access to the gallery via a single authorisation valid for the entire app, preceded by a generic notice requesting enabling of other features, which did not allow users to understand that they were also authorising suggestions from their gallery.
The regulator said Meta would now have to seek consent by means of a separate and specific request for the feature concerned and clearly signpost what it is used for, namely that it involves access to a user’s photo gallery, as well as how to disable it.
In determining the size of the fine, the authority said it took into account “the high number of people affected” – about 20 million Android users in Italy – and the duration of the infringement, “which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system”.
The authority also cited “Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation”.
It imposed a fine amounting to roughly 0.4% of the group’s annual turnover, which hit $201bn in 2025, for a net profit of $60.5bn.

A425.text:
SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.
The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.
Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights.
The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.
Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.
The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.
“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.
It was also only the second time Starship has entered Earth’s orbit.
The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.
“Making more believers by the day,” wrote Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman on X, praising the 15th flight. “One step closer to [the moon].” Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead Nasa.
SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes. Musk has touted the rocket’s reusability as a way to reel in the enormous costs of space travel.
Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.
Starship’s advances have also aided the expansion of Musk’s satellite internet empire. The spacecraft deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites during this recent flight.

A64.text:
La empresa Space X, del multimillonario y ex funcionario de Estados Unidos Elon Musk, anunció este sábado que la nave Starship logró regresar a la Tierra y fue atrapada en el aire por unos gigantescos brazos mecánicos en el mismo lugar donde comenzó su viaje 22 horas antes.
El regreso se convirtió en un hito para la compañía que dijo haber concretado la primera captura en la historia de una Starship que volvía volando desde el espacio. Pero, como el propulsor de primera etapa explotó poco después del despegue del viernes desde Texas, la empresa no logró su ansiada doble captura, que sigue siendo el objetivo para acelerar los viajes a la Luna y Marte.
Los restos permanecían en el Golfo de México, acordonados con boyas, mientras la nave espacial de acero inoxidable, con forma de bala, descendía en posición vertical hasta la plataforma de lanzamiento.
La dramática captura, digna de un relato de ciencia ficción, ayudó a eclipsar el fallido y desordenado intento con el propulsor. Las cámaras recorrieron la nave de arriba abajo mientras quedaba suspendida muy por encima del suelo, sostenida por los brazos de la torre de lanzamiento.
“¿Pueden creerlo?”, gritó el comentarista de SpaceX Dan Huot, alargando cada palabra. “¡Mírenla! ¡Cariño, está de vuelta!”
Congratulations to an incredible team at SpaceX!!! pic.twitter.com/phiZ0amQyp
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 14, 2026
Poco después, Elon Musk felicitó a su “increíble equipo”. Funcionarios de SpaceX indicaron que la captura del sábado demuestra la reutilización total de Starship, lo cual es crucial para un reciclaje rápido y de bajo costo. Aunque la recuperación del propulsor del viernes fracasó, la empresa ya había logrado tres capturas previas de propulsores, lo que valida la técnica.
La NASA celebró la noticia
La agencia espacial del gobierno de los Estados Unidos paga miles de millones de dólares para que Starship alunice con astronautas de Artemis más adelante en esta década y ayude a construir una base lunar permanente. Las ambiciones de Musk son aún mayores: quiere lanzar una flota de Starships para construir una ciudad en Marte.
“Fue casi magia”, manifestó el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, a través de X. “Sumando más creyentes cada día... un paso más cerca de (emojis de la Luna y la bandera de Estados Unidos)”.
El cohete, un coloso de 124 metros, despegó a última hora de la tarde del viernes desde la base Starship de SpaceX cerca de la frontera entre Estados Unidos y México. Tras separarse limpiamente de su propulsor antes de que las cosas se torcieran, la nave de la etapa superior se elevó hasta la órbita y liberó 26 satélites Starlink avanzados.
Starship continuó dando vueltas alrededor del mundo a 265 kilómetros de altura, con vistas en directo de sí misma y de la Tierra transmitidas mediante Starlink. La nave completó 14 vueltas alrededor de la Tierra, superando con creces la misión anterior, que dio de una a dos vueltas.
Fue el 15to vuelo de SpaceX de una Starship a escala real desde 2023 y apenas su segundo viaje a la órbita.
SpaceX informó que todos los elementos de la nave, incluido su vital escudo térmico, parecían haber funcionado bien.
En cuanto al propulsor, Kate Tice, de SpaceX, explicó que sus motores dejaron de impulsar demasiado pronto durante el descenso. El sistema de guiado del propulsor detectó que no estaba en la posición correcta e inició automáticamente el desvío hacia el agua y la autodestrucción. Los ingenieros aún investigan la causa.
SpaceX espera comenzar a lanzar Starships desde el Centro Espacial Kennedy, en Florida, en los próximos meses. Ese es el punto de partida de la próxima misión Artemis de la NASA, que no alunizará y permanecerá en órbita alrededor de la Tierra para practicar con el módulo de alunizaje.
Los cuatro astronautas de Artemis III intentarán acoplar su cápsula no solo con Starship, sino también con Blue Moon, de Blue Origin. Las dos compañías se alternarán para llevar tripulaciones a la superficie lunar.

A85.text:
Israelischer Luftangriff Hamas-Kommandeur im Gazastreifen getötet
Das israelische Militär hat nach eigenen Angaben einen ranghohen Kommandeur des bewaffneten Arms der Hamas angegriffen. Bei dem Luftangriff in Chan Junis im Süden des Gazastreifens sei Samir Abu Younis getötet worden, erfuhr die Nachrichtenagentur Reuters aus Hamas-Kreisen.
Sanitätern zufolge wurden dabei weitere Menschen verletzt. Die Hamas bestätigte später den Tod von Abu Younis. Die Beerdigung solle am Sonntagnachmittag in Chan Junis stattfinden, teilte die Organisation mit.
Der 53-Jährige befehligte die Rafah-Brigade. Er gehörte seit 1991 den Qassam-Brigaden an und hatte in Rafah mehrere Führungsposten inne. 
Seit Oktober 2025 gilt im Gazastreifen eigentlich eine Waffenruhe, die die schweren Kämpfe beenden soll. Sie hat jedoch weder die israelischen Angriffe gestoppt noch eine Entwaffnung der Hamas herbeigeführt.
Sechs Tote nach Luftangriff auf Klinik
Erst am Donnerstag hatte Israel ein Krankenhaus im Süden des Gazastreifens angegriffen. Dabei wurden nach palästinensischen Angaben mindestens sechs Menschen getötet, darunter ein Chirurg. 20 weitere Menschen seien verletzt worden, teilte ein Sprecher der Gaza-Zivilschutzbehörde mit.
Ein Hamas-Sprecher verurteilte den Angriff als Kriegsverbrechen. Das israelische Militär erklärte, der Einsatz habe einem ranghohen Hamas-Mitglied und weiteren Kämpfern gegolten. Die Armee warf der militanten Palästinenser-Organisation vor, den Klinikkomplex unter anderem als Kommandozentrum und Waffenlager zu nutzen. Die Angaben ließen sich nicht unabhängig überprüfen.
Das angegriffene Krankenhaus ist das Nasser-Hospital in Chan Junis, eine der größten Kliniken im Gazastreifen, der durch den Krieg weitgehend zerstört ist. Nach Angaben des Zivilschutz-Sprechers wurde die chirurgische Abteilung getroffen.
Nach Angaben der Gaza-Behörden wurden seit Beginn der Waffenruhe im Oktober 2025 mindestens 1600 Palästinenser in dem Küstenstreifen getötet. Israel meldete im selben Zeitraum vier getötete Soldaten. Auslöser des Krieges war das Massaker der Hamas in Israel im Oktober 2023, bei dem nach israelischen Angaben etwa 1200 Menschen getötet wurden. Israel reagierte mit einer groß angelegten Militäroffensive, durch die nach palästinensischen Angaben insgesamt mehr als 74.000 Menschen getötet wurden.
Im vierten Winter seit Kriegsbeginn sterben in Gaza wieder Menschen infolge von Kälte, Niederschlag und Sturm. So wie die Familie von Ahmed Nabhan. Das ist weniger Folge der widrigen Natur – als vor allem der Politik .

A96.text:
Ukraine: Zelenskyy says security deal could go to referendum
November 14, 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US peace envoys asked whether Kyiv would withdraw from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, according to remarks to the media published on Saturday.
The suggestion was made following the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi to bring Russia's nearly 5-year war in Ukraine to a close.
What did Zelenskyy say?
The Ukrainian leader told reporters: "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'"
Zelenskyy repeated Kyiv's position that it was not willing to cede territory to Russia. But he added that if the country reached a comprehensive deal, including security guarantees, a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to the public in a referendum.
"That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Zelenskyy said the prospect of NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas has not been raised before.
He also warned about Moscow's plan to change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.
Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.
"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.
"Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."
Europe to play bigger role in peace talks
On Friday, the EU said several European diplomats would take part in future Ukraine peace talks, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland.
Moscow has long insisted that European states be excluded from the negotiations because they support Ukraine.
Russian forces strike Zaporizhzhia
The comments come as Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had captured the settlement of Tersianka in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, news agency Interfax reported.
Interfax cited the ministry as saying that Russian forces had struck Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure used by the military, along with ammunition depots and drone production and storage sites.
Russia has targeted power stations across Ukraine in waves of ballistic and cruise missile attacks, cutting power and heating to millions of people as temperatures plunge.
Zelenskyy warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's war campaign, which Kyiv insists is aimed at hurting public morale.
